meta.title: skills-ef
meta.tagline: A simple, repeatable way of working with Claude — for finance, files, code, and the writing around them.
meta.intro_lead: Each skill does one job well, and they fit together into a loop you can learn once and reuse everywhere.

sections.title: Overview
sections.kicker: A simple, repeatable way of working with Claude
sections.sub: For finance, files, code, and the writing around them. You don't need to be technical — every skill has a plain-language card with an everyday example, and the search box above jumps to anything by name.
sections.note: Two tracks share the same four steps — Folders and Workbook — and both run end to end; bigger work has its own flow further down the page.

sections.title: Everyday tools — reach for them anytime
sections.blurb: Not steps in any flow — self-contained tools you use on their own whenever they help: session summaries, titles, polished messages, plus the pieces for setting up and maintaining the system itself.

sections.title: Helpers Claude weaves in
sections.blurb: Claude weaves these into the loop and the bigger-work flow further down the page — and you can reach for any of them yourself, at any stage. They're never stops you ride through.

sections.title: The workflow loop
sections.blurb: Most work follows the same four-step shape: get your bearings, make a plan, do the work carefully, then close it out. Learn this once and it applies whether you're working in a folder of files or an Excel workbook. Every branch is a skill — click one to open its card; each track's full story is drawn in its own section below.

stages.title: 1 · Explore
stages.blurb: Get your bearings — what's here, what's in progress, what to do next.

stages.title: 2 · Plan
stages.blurb: Decide the approach before touching anything — and name the checks that prove it worked.

stages.title: 3 · Build
stages.blurb: Do the work one step at a time, verifying as you go and confirming before anything risky.

stages.title: 4 · Log
stages.blurb: Record what changed as durable history and update the status.

sections.title: The Folders loop, up close
sections.blurb: The tree above teaches the shared four-step shape; this is how a folder task actually rides it. The extra machinery is what carries between sessions: the in-flight signal build opens and log completes, the three signs of unfinished work explore checks when you return, and the door at plan for work too big for one session. Click any stop to open its card.

stubArc.label: LOG.md stub
stubArc.detail: build opens it · log completes it

chip.label: settled a structural decision? · → docs/adr/ (offered, gated)

caps: The whole loop speaks the folder's own vocabulary: when a GLOSSARY.md glossary exists, plan and build use its canonical terms, and log records any term the work sharpened — a folder only earns a glossary when it has words worth pinning.

Big reorganizations get sliced: plan orders the work as thin end-to-end units — move the files, rewire what points at them, check it worked — and build closes each slice before opening the next, so a wrong turn surfaces after one slice, not after all of them.

History is chosen once, at onboarding: Git by default, a LOG.md file for a named reason. The loop adapts — on Git the dirty working tree is the in-flight signal and the record is a commit; on a file-based folder, the stub drawn above is the signal and the completed entry is the record.

The docs/adr/ deposit drawn at log isn't log's alone: folder-onboarding makes the same offer when a first visit surfaces a settled structural decision — both gated the same way, and the default is no offer.

sections.title: The Workbook loop, up close
sections.blurb: The tree above teaches the shared four-step shape; this is how an Excel workbook task actually rides it. Here the between-sessions machinery lives inside the workbook itself: the in-flight stub plan writes to the Audit Log and log completes at close, the Handoff sheet that carries a paused task to the next session, and the two audits waiting beside the line for when the numbers deserve a harder look. Click any stop to open its card.

stubArc.label: In-progress stub
stubArc.detail: plan writes it to the Audit Log · log completes it in place

siding.title: Audit escalation — in order
siding.note: escalation targets, not stops on the line

shelf.title: Composed in when needed — reference know-how
shelf.note: plan names the reference skills the task calls for and build inherits them: background know-how Claude draws on while it works. None of these are stops you ride through.

caps: The arcs above ride two of the workbook's four AI-scaffolding sheets — the Audit Log the stub lives on, and the Handoff sheet the triangle carries between sessions. The other two work every phase without an arc of their own: the Instructions sheet is the workbook's human manual and vocabulary, and the Agent sheet holds the standing guidance, active risks, and open decisions a session reads before acting.

Explore's Full orientation is the deep read for when you'll do real work — and it ends by offering /grill-with-files, which stress-tests the plan against the workbook's actual contents instead of your memory of them.

Close-out is more than the log entry: workbook-log refreshes the Workbook Snapshot only when the task materially changed what it reports, and proposes Agent-sheet updates only when the work surfaced standing guidance — "nothing to propose" is the common, correct outcome.
sections.alsoCardsLabel: The toolkit drawn beside it — audits, handoff & reference know-how

sections.title: Building small apps & tools — the code side
sections.blurb: Sometimes the work is software itself — a small app or tool to build, a bug to hunt down, a codebase to tidy up. These skills bring the same careful, plan-first way of working to code: some you run yourself, and the rest Claude reaches for automatically.

sections.title: Bigger work — from idea to shipped
sections.blurb: Bigger work follows one shape: shape the idea, decide whether it's a multi-session build, then build it — implement builds code; the Folders and Workbook loops build what lives in a folder or a workbook. Step one is a choice: grill-with-docs shapes an idea that fits one session's planning; when it's too big and foggy for that, wayfinder maps it instead, and its lane skips the junction and merges back at to-spec — a wayfinder effort is multi-session by definition. ask-ef is the guide that points you to the right step in this flow; the shelf underneath holds the helpers Claude weaves in along the way. Click any skill to open its card.

flow.title: The flow at a glance

steps.label: shape
steps.detail: grill-with-docs — or wayfinder when the idea can't fit one session

steps.label: build
steps.detail: implement for code, per ticket in a fresh session, or implement-spec for the whole spec at once; the Folders or Workbook loop otherwise

steps.label: review
steps.detail: code-review closes each build; when the work goes up as a pull request, pr shapes its description; after a code build, retro looks back and suggests fixes to the setup

flow.caption: Fits one session? Skip 2–3 and build inline.

sections.routerNote: the guide that points you to the right step

spur.note: Behind the Yes door, the build-arm runs once per ticket, in fresh context: implement for code, the loop for a folder or workbook (implement-spec is the exception: it builds every ticket in one run with helper agents); each ticket names the tickets that must finish before it, so any ticket whose blockers are done can be picked up; handoff carries what matters from one ticket session to the next.

arm.name: Code
arm.label: the code arm
arm.note: implement is one skill, not a four-phase loop — it runs the whole code build: tests first at the agreed spots, checks along the way, a review at the end. The code-bench tools on the shelf below compose in.

sections.descendNote: pick the arm by what you're building — code, a folder, or a workbook

shelf.note: Claude weaves the helpers into the steps above (and you can reach for them any time) — they're never stops you ride through. The code bench backs the code arm: implement composes those tools in as it builds.

sections.title: For maintainers — how this was built
body: This page is generated: a small script reads the live list of shipping skills and merges it with hand-written teaching copy, then emits one self-contained file — so it can't drift out of date. When new skills land, re-running the script picks them up automatically.

grill-with-docs.gist: Get grilled while it captures the decisions and definitions as written records along the way.
grill-with-docs.example: Kicking off a new area of work, you make the key calls and they're saved as decision records for the next person.
grill-with-docs.whenToReach: Starting bigger, multi-session work that deserves a paper trail.

to-spec.gist: Turn a conversation you've already had into a written spec, without being re-interviewed.
to-spec.example: After talking through a new feature, you run it to capture everything you agreed on as one document the build can follow.
to-spec.whenToReach: When a decision is big enough to span multiple sessions and needs a durable spec.

to-tickets.gist: Break a plan or spec into small tickets, each naming the tickets that must finish before it can start.
to-tickets.example: A spec describes a multi-part feature; this cuts it into standalone tickets, each finishable and checkable by itself, so anything whose blockers are done can be picked up next.
to-tickets.whenToReach: When a plan is too big to do in one go and you want bite-sized tasks with a clear order.

wayfinder.gist: Plan an effort too big and foggy for one sitting by keeping a shared map of open questions, answered one at a time.
wayfinder.example: A big project's path isn't visible yet; this charts the open decisions as a map on the tracker and works through them one per session until the way is clear.
wayfinder.whenToReach: When the work is so large you can't yet see the way to the destination, let alone write the spec.

triage.gist: Move incoming requests through clear states — sort them, verify they're real, and leave a brief so the next person can act.
triage.example: A request comes in; you confirm it holds up, decide what kind it is, and write notes saying exactly what's settled and what's still needed.
triage.whenToReach: When you have a queue of requests and need to decide what's ready to work on.

ask-ef.gist: A guide that points you to the right skill when you're not sure where to start.
ask-ef.example: You have something to do but don't know which skill fits — you ask, and it routes you to the right first step.
ask-ef.whenToReach: Any time you're unsure which skill or flow to use.

setup-skills-ef.gist: A one-time setup that tells the skills where your project keeps its tasks, what its labels mean, and where its notes live.
setup-skills-ef.example: You add these skills to a new project and run setup once so the other skills know where everything is.
setup-skills-ef.whenToReach: Once, before you first use the planning and issue skills in a new project.

implement.gist: Take a finished plan — a spec or a set of issues — and build it: tests first at the agreed spots, checks run along the way, and a review at the end.
implement.example: You've sliced a feature into issues; Claude works through them in small test-first steps, running the checks as it goes, then reviews the finished work before committing.
implement.whenToReach: When planning is done and it's time to actually build — you have a spec or issues ready to become working, committed code.

implement-spec.mapLabel: builds a whole spec at once, tickets in parallel
implement-spec.gist: Build an entire spec in one run. Claude reads the tickets as a map of what waits on what, sends helper agents to work every ticket that's ready at the same time, merges their work onto one shared branch, and finishes with a review.
implement-spec.example: You've split a feature into eight tickets, some waiting on others; Claude starts the three that are free right away, picks up each next one as its blockers finish, and hands you one reviewed branch at the end.
implement-spec.whenToReach: When a spec and its tickets are ready and you want the whole thing built in one go, rather than one ticket per session with implement.

prototype.mapLabel: answers a design question with throwaway code
prototype.gist: Build a throwaway version to answer one design question — a single HTML file to poke at when the question is how it should behave, or several different looks of one screen when it's how it should look.
prototype.example: You can't picture what your app's dashboard should look like, so it builds three genuinely different versions you flip between in the browser — you keep the winner and delete the rest.
prototype.whenToReach: When a design question is easier to answer by trying it than by debating it — the code is disposable; the answer is what you keep.

improve-codebase-architecture.mapLabel: codebase upkeep that feeds ideas back into the flow
improve-codebase-architecture.gist: Scan a whole codebase for spots where the structure causes friction, then lay out the best fixes — turning many tangled little pieces into fewer solid ones — in a visual report.
improve-codebase-architecture.example: You sense every small change ripples through ten files; Claude explores the code, opens a before-and-after report in your browser, and stress-tests your chosen fix with you before anything changes.
improve-codebase-architecture.whenToReach: When the code fights you on every change and you want structural fixes weighed up, not another quick patch. Bug hunts that keep landing in the same messy corner end up here too.

retro.mapLabel: learns from a coding session to smooth the next one
retro.gist: Look back on a coding session and suggest changes to the project's setup so the next session goes better: clearer pointers to the right files, automated checks that would have caught the mistakes, sharper rules for the reviewer, and leaner standing instructions. The most serious suggestions come first.
retro.example: Claude spent half a session hunting for the right config file and let through a slip a lint check would have caught; the retro proposes a pointer in the project notes and that new check, worst problem first.
retro.whenToReach: Right after a coding session, while it's fresh, when you want the project itself to get easier for Claude to work in. It improves the setup, not the session record; to close out a session, use wrap-up.

tdd.mapLabel: test-first building at the agreed spots
tdd.gist: Build a feature or fix a bug in small proven steps — write one test that says what the code should do, add just enough code to pass it, then repeat.
tdd.example: You ask for a checkout feature; Claude writes a single failing test for the first behavior, makes it pass, then moves to the next — each step proven before the next begins.
tdd.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when you want something built or fixed test-first — and implement weaves it in at agreed points during a larger build.

code-review.mapLabel: checks finished work against the rules and the ask
code-review.gist: Review a finished chunk of work along two separate axes — does the code follow this project's written standards, and does it actually do what the issue asked? Two independent reviewers report side by side, so a pass on one can't hide a failure on the other.
code-review.example: You finish a feature branch and ask for a review since main; one reviewer flags a naming rule the project documents, the other spots a requirement from the issue that never got built — each reported on its own.
code-review.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when you ask to review a branch, a PR, or the changes since some point — and implement hands off to it when a build wraps up.

pr.mapLabel: shapes a pull request so it's quick to review
pr.gist: Write the description of a pull request (a proposed change waiting for sign-off) in one fixed shape: a small picture of what changed, before and after proof that it works, and a plain call on how risky it is to merge and how hard it would be to undo.
pr.example: Claude finishes a fix and opens a pull request; the description shows a short sketch of the changed flow, the test that failed before and passes now, and a note that the change is easy to roll back and touches only one screen.
pr.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically whenever it writes a pull request description.

codebase-design.gist: Background know-how for shaping code into deep modules — lots of behavior hidden behind a small, simple surface — so each piece is easier to use, change, and test.
codebase-design.example: You're adding a payments piece to your tool; Claude draws on this to give it one simple front door and tuck the fiddly logic behind it — sometimes sketching a few rival designs and comparing them.
codebase-design.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically whenever code is being designed or restructured — and it supplies the shared vocabulary improve-codebase-architecture leans on.

diagnosing-bugs.mapLabel: a proof-first discipline for hard bugs
diagnosing-bugs.gist: A discipline for hard bugs: before guessing at causes, build a fast, repeatable check that fails on exactly this bug — then narrow suspects one at a time until the fix proves itself.
diagnosing-bugs.example: Your app crashes on export, but only sometimes; Claude first makes the failure happen on demand, then tests a short ranked list of suspects until the real cause is caught and locked in with a test.
diagnosing-bugs.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when you report something broken, throwing errors, failing, or slow. Secrets in the commands and outputs it shows are redacted first.

research.mapLabel: reads the primary sources while you keep working
research.gist: Hand a question to a background researcher — it digs through the primary sources (official docs, source code, specs), follows every claim back to where it came from, and leaves a cited write-up in your project while you keep working.
research.example: You need to know what an API actually charges per call before building around it; Claude sends a researcher to the official docs and keeps building with you — the cited notes file arrives a few minutes later.
research.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when you want a topic researched or reading legwork delegated — the write-up it leaves is something to carry into planning, not a replacement for it.

wizard.mapLabel: a guided script for the steps only you can do
wizard.gist: Turn a manual procedure — signing up for a service, pasting in API keys, clicking through a dashboard — into a step-by-step script that opens each page, tells you what to copy, and files the values where they belong.
wizard.example: A new project needs three third-party accounts and their keys in place; Claude writes a wizard that walks you through each one and saves the secrets, so nobody re-explains the setup next time.
wizard.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when it hits a step a human has to do by hand; run it yourself for any setup, migration, or cutover you'd otherwise narrate to an agent.

folder-explore.gist: Get your bearings in a folder at the start of a session — it checks the state and offers you the right next step.
folder-explore.example: You open a project folder you haven't touched in weeks and need to know what's there and what's unfinished.
folder-explore.whenToReach: At the start of any session working in a folder.

folder-pickup.gist: A quick catch-up on a folder you've worked in before — the essentials, then it stops.
folder-pickup.example: You're back in a familiar folder and just want a short 'what changed, anything in progress?' summary.
folder-pickup.whenToReach: Returning to a folder you've already set up.

folder-onboarding.gist: Open a brand-new folder and make it understandable — it writes a plain-English guide plus working notes, and starts tracking history.
folder-onboarding.example: Someone hands you a messy shared drive and says 'make sense of this' — this documents what's there and how it's organized.
folder-onboarding.whenToReach: The first time you set a folder up for ongoing work.

folder-plan.gist: Draft a clear plan before you move or change a batch of files — goal, steps, and the checks that prove it worked.
folder-plan.example: Before reorganizing a folder and updating links across many files, you lay out the plan so a wrong turn gets caught early.

folder-build.gist: Carry out a folder plan carefully — one step at a time, checking as it goes and asking before anything risky.
folder-build.example: Your plan is ready; this moves the files, verifies links still work, and confirms with you before deleting anything.
folder-build.whenToReach: When a folder plan is ready to execute.

folder-log.gist: Wrap up folder work — record it in the history with a clear note and refresh the folder's status.
folder-log.example: You've reorganized and updated docs; this commits everything in one tidy, well-described checkpoint.
folder-log.whenToReach: When you finish a unit of folder work.

grill-me.mapLabel: the same grilling, from memory — no files needed
grill-me.gist: Start the relentless grilling interview to stress-test a plan or design before you build.
grill-me.example: Before a big reorganization, you have it poke holes in your approach so you fix them now, not later.
grill-me.whenToReach: When you want to pressure-test a plan from memory — no files needed.

grilling.mapLabel: the engine under every grill step
grilling.gist: Reach clarity on a decision before you start — it works through every angle, asking a round of questions at a time and recommending an answer for each.
grilling.example: Designing something with lots of moving parts, you walk each decision to a clear answer before starting.
grilling.whenToReach: The engine behind the grill skills — reach for it when you want the full design-tree interview.

grill-with-files.mapLabel: grills your plan against the real files
grill-with-files.gist: Stress-test a plan against the actual files it touches — it opens them and challenges you with what's really there.
grill-with-files.example: Before editing a workbook or restructuring a folder, it reads the real contents and catches problems instead of asking you to describe them.
grill-with-files.whenToReach: When the plan touches files and you want it grounded in what's on disk.

handoff.gist: Write a session summary the next agent can trust — stated facts only (what you confirmed this session, not guesses), pointing at prior docs instead of duplicating them.
handoff.example: After a long working session, you write a standalone brief of what's settled, what's still a lead, and what comes next.
handoff.whenToReach: When you need to pause and hand off cleanly, so the next session resumes without re-deriving or inheriting wrong assumptions.

domain-modeling.gist: Pin down what your project's words actually mean, and record the big decisions as you make them.
domain-modeling.example: You realize a term means different things to different people, so you write down the one precise definition everyone will use.
domain-modeling.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when you're discussing a project's terminology or writing or editing a GLOSSARY.md or an ADR; reach for it yourself when fuzzy terms or undocumented decisions are causing confusion.

daily-note.gist: Turn a work session into a short, skimmable summary for your manager — the outcomes, not the play-by-play.
daily-note.example: End of day, you capture what you solved in a few lines your manager can read in fifteen seconds.
daily-note.whenToReach: When you want a quick, manager-facing recap of what got done.

chat-title.gist: Give the current chat a short, clear title that's easy to spot in the sidebar list.
chat-title.example: After a working session, you have it name the chat by what it accomplished so you can find it later in a crowded project list.
chat-title.whenToReach: When you want the current chat labeled by its outcome, so it's easy to find later.

retitle-sessions.gist: Batch-fix the titles of past chats so your sidebar tells you at a glance what each old session did.
retitle-sessions.example: Your project list is full of vague or auto-generated titles, so you run it to get a table of better names for the bad ones and apply the ones you like.
retitle-sessions.whenToReach: When your list of past chats has gone stale and you want to retitle the worst offenders in one pass.

work-coms.gist: Polish a rough draft or brain-dump into a clean, professional message in your own voice.
work-coms.example: You paste your rough thoughts for a reply and get back a clear, ready-to-send message matched to the channel.
work-coms.whenToReach: When you need to send a polished email or chat message fast.

meeting-notes.gist: Turn a raw meeting transcript into a clean debrief: what happened, what was decided, and who owes what — never inventing what it can't hear.
meeting-notes.example: You paste a punctuation-free voice-memo transcript and get back a saved debrief with decisions and action items, unclear spots flagged instead of guessed.
meeting-notes.whenToReach: When a meeting recording or transcript needs to become notes and action items.

teach.gist: Learn a new topic over several sessions, with lessons and a learning path that remembers your progress.
teach.example: You want to get good at a topic, so it sets up a workspace and walks you through it step by step over time.
teach.whenToReach: When you want to learn something gradually, not in one sitting.

to-questionnaire.gist: When the answer lives in someone else's head, write them a questionnaire — Claude asks you only who it's for and what you need back, then aims the questions at the gap.
to-questionnaire.example: You can't finish the plan without the operations lead's numbers, so you send a one-page questionnaire they fill in on their own time.
to-questionnaire.whenToReach: When a decision is blocked on knowledge you don't have and one person does.

wait-what.gist: A one-line reset for when a reply didn't land: Claude re-pitches it in plain language with the context you were missing.
wait-what.example: Mid-session the explanation went over your head; you type it and get the same point again, shorter and in your project's own vocabulary.
wait-what.whenToReach: The moment a message doesn't land, inside any other skill.

unslop.gist: Strip the tells that make a piece of writing read as machine-made (puffery, filler, em dashes, chatbot sign-offs) and sharpen the voice that is already there, without changing what the text says.
unslop.example: You paste a draft email that reads like a bot wrote it; you get it back saying the same things in plain words, in your register, with nothing invented.
unslop.whenToReach: Any draft, doc, or message that needs to sound like a person before it goes out.

wrap-up.gist: An end-of-session ritual: Claude accounts for everything the session changed, writes a short where-things-stand summary, and proposes anything worth keeping — nothing is written until you approve.
wrap-up.example: You finish an afternoon of work and type it; you get Done / Where it stands / Open / Next, plus one proposed lesson to save for future sessions — you say yes or no to each.
wrap-up.whenToReach: Ending any session; a finished workbook or folder task runs its own close-out first.

rewrite-skill.gist: Rewrite one skill the way the style guide asks, in one sitting: gather what's true about it, settle the two calls only you can make, find the one rule its sections keep restating, and ship the change.
rewrite-skill.example: A skill has grown long and repeats itself; you run this on it and end the session with a shorter skill that states its rule once, plus the pull request that ships it.
rewrite-skill.whenToReach: When a skill in this repo reads badly and you want it rewritten properly, not just trimmed.

writing-for-agents.gist: The style guide for writing anything an agent reads — skills, a CLAUDE.md, a pointed-at doc — so it stays short, predictable, and reached at the right moment.
writing-for-agents.example: You're writing or tidying a skill and want to know what to keep in the file, what to push behind a pointer, and which words make the agent behave the same way every run.
writing-for-agents.whenToReach: Claude reaches for it automatically when a skill or CLAUDE.md is being created or edited; reach for it yourself when you're authoring one.

git-guardrails.gist: Set up guardrails that block risky version-control commands before they can run.
git-guardrails.example: You want to work in a project without worrying that a destructive command slips through.
git-guardrails.whenToReach: When you want a safety net against dangerous git operations.

workbook-explore.gist: Get oriented in an Excel finance workbook at the start of a session, and find the right next step.
workbook-explore.example: You open a cash-flow workbook for the first time this week and need to know what's unfinished.
workbook-explore.whenToReach: At the start of a session in a finance workbook.

workbook-onboarding.gist: Read a new workbook end to end and document how it works, so anyone can use it later.
workbook-onboarding.example: You inherit a complex variance workbook and write up how its sheets and numbers flow.
workbook-onboarding.whenToReach: The first time you take on a workbook you'll work in repeatedly — for return visits, use workbook-pickup instead.

workbook-pickup.gist: Quick re-orientation for a workbook you've worked in — read the existing notes, give a short summary, flag anything in-flight, then stop (it won't propose extra work).
workbook-pickup.example: You return to a monthly reconciliation and want a short 'what changed' summary.
workbook-pickup.whenToReach: Returning to a workbook you've already onboarded.

workbook-plan.gist: Draft a clear plan before changing a finance workbook — goal, steps, and the tie-out checks that prove the numbers still balance.
workbook-plan.example: Before reworking a reconciliation's formulas, you lay out the plan and the checks so a mistake gets caught before it ships.

workbook-build.gist: Carry out a workbook plan carefully — step by step, running the tie-out checks as you go and confirming before anything risky.
workbook-build.example: Your plan is ready; this makes the changes and verifies the totals still reconcile before you call it done.
workbook-build.whenToReach: When a workbook plan is ready to execute.

workbook-log.gist: Close out a workbook task — write it to the Audit Log sheet as a dated record, and capture any standing guidance worth keeping.
workbook-log.example: You've finished a reconciliation change; this records what changed, the checks you ran, and anything the next person should know.
workbook-log.whenToReach: When you finish a unit of work in a finance workbook.

formula-audit.gist: A fast mechanical check of a workbook's formulas — it hunts for errors, numbers typed into formulas, broken links, and ranges that miss a row, and lists what it finds.
formula-audit.example: Before sending a model, you run it to catch a stray error cell, a hardcoded figure buried in a formula, or a total that skips the last line.
formula-audit.whenToReach: As a quick check before you send a workbook, or any time you want to sanity-check a sheet's formulas.

logic-audit.gist: Decode the business logic hidden in a workbook's formulas — how raw records get sorted into the reported numbers — and check it's complete, doesn't double-count, and ties out.
logic-audit.example: You suspect a report quietly misses a category or counts something twice; this maps the rules behind the numbers and flags the gaps or overlaps.
logic-audit.whenToReach: When the reasoning behind the numbers lives in formulas you can't easily read. Run formula-audit first to rule out mechanical errors.

workbook-handoff.gist: Pause a workbook task cleanly mid-stream — it writes a Handoff note inside the workbook so the next session, or the next person, picks up exactly where you left off.
workbook-handoff.example: You have to stop partway through a reconciliation; this records what's done, what's left, and what to watch, so resuming doesn't start from scratch.
